author: Tertullian
addressee: Christians, especially those facing questions about how to earn a living and participate in public life without falling into idolatry
occasion: Tertullian writes to warn Christians that idolatry is far broader than offering sacrifice to idols. He addresses believers who excuse their involvement in trades, teaching, public office, military service, festivals, and oaths connected with pagan religion, arguing that such participation compromises the faith.
argument: Idolatry is the chief sin of the human race and includes every other major crime. It is not limited to sacrificing to idols but extends to making or decorating idols, teaching pagan literature, astrology, trading in goods used for idol worship, holding public office with its idolatrous trappings, military service, celebrating pagan festivals, and even swearing or being blessed by pagan gods. Christians must avoid every contact with idolatry, even at the cost of livelihood or social standing, because faith in God cannot be shared with demons. The treatise ends by urging believers to examine themselves and warning that idolaters have no place in the church, just as no unclean animal was in Noah's ark.

outline.move: Idolatry is the chief sin, containing within itself all other major crimes such as murder, adultery, fraud, and falsehood.
Idolatry must be understood broadly, as the Lord broadened adultery and murder to include inward dispositions, not just outward acts.
The origin and meaning of the word 'idol' shows that every form or image made for worship falls under idolatry.
Scripture, including Enoch and Isaiah, condemns both the makers and the worshippers of idols.
Tertullian answers excuses from idol-makers, including the plea of poverty and the appeal to Paul's teaching about working with one's hands.
Making idols contradicts the Christian renunciation of the devil, and the maker worships the idol with his own soul and labor.
It is a scandal for idol-makers to be admitted to church office, since their hands daily offend the body of Christ.
Trades that build or decorate temples and idol-related structures share in the crime, though Christians may practice related crafts that serve ordinary human needs.
Astrology and magic are condemned as idolatrous, and the visit of the magi does not excuse them after the gospel.
Schoolteachers and professors of literature are entangled in idolatry because they must teach pagan gods and observe pagan festivals; believers may learn but should not teach.
Trade that supplies idol worship, such as the frankincense seller, is idolatrous, just as aiding any forbidden act makes one guilty of it.
The plea of poverty is answered by the Lord's teaching on trusting God and leaving all for discipleship.
Christians must not share in pagan festivals, gift-days, or the joys of the world, since light has no communion with darkness.
The fear of blasphemy is no excuse for joining pagan celebrations; true pleasing of others is by virtue, not by sharing in idolatry.
Decorating doors with lamps and laurels for public festivals honors door-gods and is idolatry; Christians must render to Caesar only what is Caesar's.
Tertullian offers his opinion that private ceremonies such as coming-of-age, betrothal, and marriage are not inherently idolatrous, but Christians must avoid the sacrifices attached to them.
Slaves, freedmen, and officials must not assist in sacrifices; Tertullian doubts that holding public office is possible while avoiding every idolatrous duty.
The insignia of public office are dedicated to idols, and touching anything from the pomp of the devil is itself idolatry.
Military service is incompatible with the divine oath and the sign of Christ, since no one can serve both God and Caesar.
Christians must avoid naming pagan gods as gods and must not swear by them, even in common expressions.
Allowing oneself to be bound by an oath in the name of pagan gods, or responding in kind to such curses, is idolatry.
Receiving a blessing in the name of pagan gods is a curse by God, and hiding one's faith for the sake of a benefit is a form of denial.
Writing a sworn pledge while claiming not to have spoken is still swearing, since the mind dictates what the hand writes.
The treatise concludes with a call to vigilance, self-examination, and the warning that idolaters have no place in the church.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher in Carthage writing to warn believers against idolatry.

cast.name: Enoch
cast.who: Ancient prophet quoted as predicting that all elements of the world would be turned into idols.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: Old Testament prophet quoted against makers and worshippers of idols.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Lawgiver who forbade making idols but made the bronze serpent at God's command.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: Old Testament figure who held high office in Babylon while avoiding idolatry.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: Old Testament figure who administered Egypt while remaining free from idolatry.

cast.name: Simon Magus
cast.who: Magician who believed but was cursed by the apostles for trying to buy the Holy Spirit.

cast.name: Sergius Paulus
cast.who: Roman proconsul whom the magician opposed; the magician himself was struck blind, not Sergius Paulus.

cast.name: Herod
cast.who: King who sought the infant Christ; mentioned in the discussion of the magi.

cast.name: Nebuchadnezzar
cast.who: Babylonian king whose image the three brothers refused to honor.

cast.name: Darius
cast.who: King whom Daniel served faithfully while avoiding idolatry.

cast.name: Zechariah
cast.who: Father of John the Baptist, who wrote his son's name when struck mute.

cast.name: Eleazar
cast.who: The poor man in the parable who received comfort in Abraham's bosom.

cast.name: John the Apostle
cast.who: Apostle who taught that whoever hates his brother is a murderer; also the son of Zebedee who left his father and boat when called by the Lord.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: The Baptist who gave soldiers a rule of conduct.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: Apostle whom the Lord disarmed, symbolizing the end of military service for Christians.

cast.name: Matthew
cast.who: Tax collector called by the Lord from his booth.

cast.name: James
cast.who: Apostle, brother of John and son of Zebedee, who left his father and boat when called by the Lord.

cast.name: Aaron
cast.who: Old Testament priest who carried a buckle, mentioned in the discussion of military equipment.

cast.name: Joshua
cast.who: Old Testament leader who led the people in war.

cast.name: Marcionites
cast.who: Heretics who accused God of inconsistency between the law and later commands.

key_terms.sense: The worship or service of idols in any form, including making, decorating, supplying, or honoring them
Any form or image made for worship, from the Greek eidos meaning form
A likeness or statue made as an object of worship
Unclean spirits to whom idols are dedicated and who receive the worship given to idols
Craftsmen who make idols or anything used in idol worship
Offerings made to idols, which Christians must not attend or support
The display and trappings of worldly power and honor, which belong to the devil and which Christians renounced at baptism
The Christian rule of life and teaching that separates believers from pagan practice
Non-Christian pagans, the nations who worship idols
Things offered or dedicated to idols, including festivals and goods connected with idol worship
The Christian oath or pledge of faith, especially the baptismal renunciation of the devil
A dealer in frankincense used for idol sacrifices
Astrologers who claim to read fate from the stars, associated with fallen angels
A schoolteacher who instructs children in literature, necessarily teaching pagan myths and festivals
Military service, which requires an oath and acts incompatible with Christian allegiance

scripture: Tertullian uses the Septuagint and Old Latin versions, citing Old Testament books by their Greek/Latin names (e.g., 'Esaias' for Isaiah, 'Moyses' for Moses, 'Iesus Naue' for Joshua). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where they differ. New Testament citations follow the Old Latin, with sayings of Jesus and Paul quoted loosely from memory.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Tertullian's career is uncertain, though it is generally placed in his later, more rigorist period.
The precise identity of the 'brother' mentioned in section 15 as having a vision is unknown.
The exact wording of some Old Latin scriptural quotations is uncertain due to textual variants in the manuscript tradition.
Whether Tertullian wrote this before or after his association with Montanism is debated.

_unresolved_facts.fix: Sergius Paulus: Roman proconsul who was with the magician; the magician himself was struck blind for opposing the apostles, not Sergius Paulus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: John the Apostle: Apostle who taught that whoever hates his brother is a murderer; also the son of Zebedee who left his father and boat when called by the Lord.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ["11"], move: "Trade that supplies idol worship, such as the frankincense seller, is idolatrous, just as aiding any forbidden act makes one guilty of it."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: si, antequam idola in saeculo essent, his mercibus adhuc informis idololatria transigebatur, si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur, ecquid maioris operae et erga daemonia turarius?
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ["11"], move: "Trade that supplies idol worship, especially the frankincense seller (turarius), is idolatrous; the frankincense seller may be more deeply involved with demons than even idol-makers, since idolatry can more easily occur without an idol than without frankincense."

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ["17"], move: "Slaves, freedmen, and officials must not assist in sacrifices; Tertullian doubts that holding public office is possible while avoiding every idolatrous duty."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: si haec credibile est fieri posse
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ["17"], move: "Slaves, freedmen, and officials must not assist in sacrifices; Tertullian allows that one might hold office if completely free from idolatrous duties, though he doubts this is credible/possible ('si haec credibile est fieri posse')."

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ["18"], move: "The insignia of public office are dedicated to idols, and touching anything from the pomp of the devil is itself idolatry."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: simplex igitur purpura illa nec iam dignitatis erat, sed ingenuitatis apud barbaros insigne
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ["18"], move: "The insignia of public office are dedicated to idols, and touching anything from the pomp of the devil is itself idolatry; however, simple purple and similar marks of free birth (not power) may be distinguished, as with Joseph and Daniel."

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ["19"], move: "Military service is incompatible with the divine oath and the sign of Christ, since no one can serve both God and Caesar."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: non conuenit sacramento diuino et humano, signo Christi et signo diaboli, castris lucis et castris tenebrarum; non potest una anima duobus deberi, deo et Caesari
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections: ["19"], move: "Military service is incompatible with the divine oath and the sign of Christ, the camp of light with the camp of darkness; one soul cannot be owed to two masters, God and Caesar."
